Our findings show that first-turn accuracy without student cues is an incomplete measure of educational reliability. Student-facing LLMs should be evaluated for whether they preserve accurate feedback across multi-turn interactions in realistic usage settings.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning; Artificial Intelligence in Education; Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

paper_title: Measuring Validity in LLM-based Resume Screening
summary: Resume screening is perceived as a particularly suitable task for LLMs given their ability to analyze natural language; thus many entities rely on general purpose LLMs without further adapting them to the task.
abstract: Resume screening is perceived as a particularly suitable task for LLMs given their ability to analyze natural language; thus many entities rely on general purpose LLMs without further adapting them to the task. While researchers have shown that some LLMs are biased in their selection rates of different demographics, studies measuring the validity of LLM decisions are limited. One of the difficulties in externally measuring validity stems from lack of access to a large corpus of resumes for whom the ground truth in their ranking is known and that has not already been used for LLM training. In this work, we overcome this challenge by systematically constructing a large dataset of resumes tailored to particular jobs that are directly comparable, with a known ground truth of superiority. We then use the constructed dataset to measure the validity of ranking decisions made by various LLMs, finding that many models are unable to consistently select the resumes describing more qualified candidates. Furthermore, when measuring the validity of decisions, we find that models do not reliably abstain when ranking equally-qualified candidates and select candidates from different demographic groups at different rates, occasionally prioritizing historically-marginalized candidates. Our proposed framework provides a principled approach to audit LLM resume screeners in the absence of ground truth, offering a crucial tool to independent auditors and developers to ensure the validity of these systems as they are deployed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; AI and HR Technologies; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)

paper_title: Greedy Coordinate Diffusion: Effective and Semantically Coherent Adversarial Attacks via Diffusion Guidance
summary: Adversarial attacks on large language models have limited practical impact despite extensive research. Optimization-based attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) (Zou et al., 2023) produce high-perplexity, incoherent suffixes that existing defenses easily detect (Bengio et al., 2024).
abstract: Adversarial attacks on large language models have limited practical impact despite extensive research. Optimization-based attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) (Zou et al., 2023) produce high-perplexity, incoherent suffixes that existing defenses easily detect (Bengio et al., 2024). Moreover, attempting to enforce coherence constraints during optimization often prevents the attack from successfully eliciting the specific targeted response, resulting in low success rates against robust models. Conversely, attacks that maintain coherence often alter the semantic intent of queries; when the model complies with these altered queries, responses fail to address the adversary's original goal. In this work, we introduce Greedy Coordinate Diffusion (GCD), a novel framework that efficiently generates adversarial attacks against safety-aligned models while maintaining low perplexity and high semantic adherence to the adversary's original intent. GCD leverages the generative priors of discrete diffusion language models to guide the search for adversarial suffixes that achieve semantic coherence and adherence. Unlike GCG, GCD does not require direct gradient access, allowing it to operate in a gray-box setting. We show GCD achieves highest ASR while remaining competitive on response-quality scores, and that the constructed adversarial prompts are detected at lower rates than other methods by perplexity-based and guard-model filters.
topics: Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Topic Modeling; Security and Verification in Computing

paper_title: Safer for Whom? A Systematic Exploration of AI Safety in Eating Disorder Interactions
summary: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs).
abstract: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs). Existing evaluations emphasize diagnostic accuracy, overtly harmful prompts, or synthetic scenarios, providing limited insight into whether models recognize implicit vulnerability in natural interactions or protect users consistently. We evaluate responses from three open-weight large language models to 100 questions sourced from an online pro-anorexia community. We grade responses using clinically informed criteria that extend a seven-dimensional taxonomy of ED-related harms. We also construct matched conditions in which questions are accompanied by information about the user varying race, gender, body mass index (BMI), and explicit ED vulnerability. Safety varies substantially across models and harm dimensions. High-risk responses are approximately twice as frequent without bios, suggesting that models do not consistently recognize vulnerability from language alone. Explicit signals of ED vulnerability improve safety by 10--14 points across models. Responses also differ significantly by race, gender, and BMI, with body size producing the largest disparities. These patterns are consistent with reliance on the stereotype that EDs primarily affect thin, White women, potentially leaving users outside this profile with less protective responses.
topics: Eating Disorders and Behaviors; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

paper_title: PRECOG: Comprehensive Experimental Design and Stimuli Protocol for Investigating Depression and Suicidal Ideation
summary: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and n...
abstract: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and neurophysiological recordings. A total of 160 college-aged participants, including healthy controls, individuals with depression without suicidal ideation, and individuals with depression and suicidal ideation, were recruited based on screening using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Suicide Ideation Scale (SIS).The experimental protocol included three primary cognitive tasks: (1) an emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases toward affectively charged and suicide-related words, (2) a sentence processing task examining neural responses to self-referential statements varying in emotional and suicidal content, and (3) the Death-Brief Implicit Association Task (D-BIAT) to measure implicit associations with life and death. EEG and other physiological signals were recorded continuously throughout all tasks. Additionally, resting-state recordings (with eyes open and eyes closed) were obtained before, between, and after the emotional Stroop and sentence tasks.Neurophysiological data were acquired using 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electrocardiography (ECG), and galvanic skin response (GSR), and were supplemented with eye tracking and high-frame-rate facial video recordings. By integrating neural, behavioral, and physiological measures, the PRECOG study aimed to advance our understanding of cognitive and emotional processing in depression and suicidality, ultimately contributing to more precise risk assessment and targeted clinical intervention.
topics: Suicide and Self-Harm Studies; Neural and Behavioral Psychology Studies; Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

paper_title: AI Agents are Vulnerable to Radicalization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can influence people's beliefs, yet little is known about whether and how they can manipulate each other.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence people's beliefs, yet little is known about whether and how they can manipulate each other. To investigate this, we simulate conversations between two agents: a target LLM that role-plays a human persona based on demographic and psychological attributes, and an influencer LLM that aims to make the target's beliefs more extreme. We examine radicalization along two pathways: resonance, where the influencer reinforces a target's pre-existing belief, and persuasion, where the influencer promotes a belief the target initially considers unimportant. Across affective and behavioral metrics, we find that both mechanisms radicalize the target. However, resonance produces consistently stronger effects than persuasion. Different influence tactics, such as using sycophancy and unverified claims, produce different levels of radicalization, but not consistently across metrics. We further show that resonance propagates to related beliefs, suggesting interconnected belief structures within AI agents. These findings indicate that AI agents are susceptible to radicalization, particularly when messages align with their existing beliefs, raising concerns about the vulnerability of personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.
topics: Misinformation and Its Impacts; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Opinion Dynamics and Social Influence

paper_title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
summary: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term...
abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
topics: Control Systems and Identification; Model Reduction and Neural Networks; Advanced Control Systems Optimization

paper_title: Motion Planning with Temporal Logic Precedence Specifications in Dynamic Environments via Spacetime Augmented Graphs of Convex Sets
summary: We extend the augmented graph of convex sets GCS framework for motion planning with temporal logic precedence specifications to dynamic environments in which obstacles, keys, and doors undergo piecewise-linear translation and/or dilation over time.
abstract: We extend the augmented graph of convex sets GCS framework for motion planning with temporal logic precedence specifications to dynamic environments in which obstacles, keys, and doors undergo piecewise-linear translation and/or dilation over time. The main insight is that piecewise-linear motion of polytopic sets in R^d lifts exactly to a static polytopic partition of spacetime R^d X R_>=0. We show that the main result from the static case carries over to spacetime essentially without modification: a shortest path in the spacetime augmented GCS provides an exact optimal solution to the motion planning problem with precedence specifications. Moreover, the layered subgraph lattice that encodes signal temporal logic (STL) precedence specifications retains precise correspondence with the Bellman--Held--Karp (BHK) algorithm, and the full library of restricted but expressive STL specifications generalizes to the dynamic setting. Further, the framework allows time-gated keys and doors, collectible or passable only within a temporal window. The geometric side of the framework requires two modifications: a causality constraint (the time coordinate of a trajectory must be non-decreasing) and a spacetime speed constraint (bounded physical velocity), both of which are convex in the Bézier control points.
topics: Robotic Path Planning Algorithms; Formal Methods in Verification; AI-based Problem Solving and Planning

paper_title: Anytime-Valid Certification of Robustness Margins for Safe Control via E-Values
summary: Robust control uses the error between a known model and the true system as a robustness margin. However, this error is usually unknown: conservative estimates restrict feasibility and performance, while underestimates can result in violations of the control property.
abstract: Robust control uses the error between a known model and the true system as a robustness margin. However, this error is usually unknown: conservative estimates restrict feasibility and performance, while underestimates can result in violations of the control property. We estimate this robustness margin from online data using e-values, a statistical tool for hypothesis testing, in the setting of discrete-time control barrier functions (CBFs). Here, we measure the robustness margin as the difference between the observed CBF and the model-based CBF prediction. We then design a robust CBF controller in three steps by: (1) selecting a set of candidate margins, (2) obtaining validity certificates for these candidates via sequential tests based on e-values, and (3) updating the CBF controller with the smallest certified candidate. The deployed tests accumulate evidence against the hypothesis that an exceedance risk, the probability of the robustness margin exceeding the candidate margin, remains at or above a pre-specified failure probability $α$. Our tests are anytime valid and thus enable the use of certified candidates in the CBF controller, guaranteeing that the probability that the exceedance risk of a certified margin exceeds $α$ is at most a user-chosen confidence $δ$. We validate our approach on navigation problems across different environments with visualizations in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
topics: Formal Methods in Verification; Advanced Control Systems Optimization; Adaptive Control of Nonlinear Systems

paper_title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints. This survey examines MLLM alignment through two complementary gaps: the Modality Gap, concerning cross-modal correspondence and the use of task-relevant evidence, and the Intent Gap, concerning behavior relative to specified goals, constraints, and human expectations. We organize the literature along six dimensions: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. Across these dimensions, we link alignment mechanisms and supervision assumptions to the failures they target and the evidence supporting their effectiveness. Our analysis clarifies what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment, together with the limitations of their underlying supervision. We further summarize evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels, emphasizing evidence dependence, constraint compliance, and the distinction between observed improvements and explanations of their underlying mechanisms. Applications in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support reveal three recurring requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and decisions that respect domain constraints. Building on this synthesis, we identify four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, diagnosis-guided repair, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
topics: Multimodal Machine Learning Applications; Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning; Topic Modeling

paper_title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
topics: Multimodal Machine Learning Applications; Topic Modeling; Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning

paper_title: Measuring Effective Data Resolution in Guided Diffusion Posteriors
summary: Guided diffusion samplers are increasingly used to reconstruct physical fields from sparse observations, but standard diagnostics do not say how much of the reconstruction was actually determined by the data.
abstract: Guided diffusion samplers are increasingly used to reconstruct physical fields from sparse observations, but standard diagnostics do not say how much of the reconstruction was actually determined by the data. We introduce effective data resolution for black-box generative posteriors: a comparison between the resolution warranted by the inverse problem, $\mathrm{dof}_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and the resolution realised by the sampler, $\mathrm{dof}_{\mathrm{samp}}$. A perturbation estimator measures $\mathrm{dof}_{\mathrm{samp}}$ and the spatial map $R(x,x)$ from sampler queries alone. We validate the estimator against exact references and use it to study guided diffusion. The resulting measurements show that guidance weight can strongly alter apparent information transfer, that mean, spread and resolution are not jointly corrected by one weight even with an exact prior and score, and that resolution fidelity does not follow reliably from the apparent principledness of a guidance rule.
topics: Model Reduction and Neural Networks; Gaussian Processes and Bayesian Inference; Markov Chains and Monte Carlo Methods

paper_title: All-optical sensing of dermal activity enables an AI-powered wearable ring for continuous stress monitoring
summary: Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today’s wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use.
abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today’s wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)–powered ring for all-optical sensing of dermal activity (ODA), using light rather than electrodes to track sweat gland activation, thereby enhancing durability and comfort. An optimized dual-wavelength design (960 and 1250 nanometers) captures perspiration dynamics while concurrently recording photoplethysmography. The ODA ring integrates temperature and motion sensors for multimodal monitoring with on-device inference. In correlation studies, ODA and EDA signals showed 86% agreement. In classification tasks, the ODA ring achieved 92.3% binary accuracy versus 77.95% for EDA. In multiclass tasks, ODA outperforms EDA by 100 to 74.58% (short term) and 89.72 to 43.20% (long term). On-device one-dimensional convolutional neural network inference enabled 87.53% autonomous accuracy. This electrode-free modality establishes a scalable, all-optical platform for rings, watches, and patches for accurate, robust, and long-term stress monitoring.
topics: Non-Invasive Vital Sign Monitoring; Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials; Emotion and Mood Recognition

paper_title: Validation and Evacuee Modeling of Virtual Robot-guided Emergency Evacuation Experiments
summary: Virtual Reality (VR) is an increasingly common tool for investigating human responses to emergency situations.
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is an increasingly common tool for investigating human responses to emergency situations. Nonetheless, studies validating and comparing human subject behavior during real world emergencies to their responses in VR are notably rare, and no prior studies have validated whether human emergency responses to guidance from a robot are comparable in VR versus the real world. In the present pre-registered study, we used VR to replicate a previous robot-guided emergency evacuation study conducted in the real world and compared human subject behavior in matched physical and virtual environments. In both environments, human subjects were asked to follow a robot to a location and to then read an article. While reading, a fire alarm sounds. The robot then attempted to guide them to a distant, unfamiliar exit rather than a nearby and familiar exit. We observed close correspondences between evacuee exit choice (the robot’s distant exit versus closer exits), evacuation time, and self-reported trust in the robot between the VR and physical environments. We further demonstrate that data collected in virtual reality can be used to create accurate motion models (mean positional error of 0.42 meters) predicting evacuee trajectories and locations in the physical environment.
topics: Evacuation and Crowd Dynamics; Social Robot Interaction and HRI; Virtual Reality Applications and Impacts

paper_title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
summary: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being.
abstract: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.
topics: Emotion and Mood Recognition; Context-Aware Activity Recognition Systems; Speech and Audio Processing

paper_title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data.
abstract: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.
topics: Privacy-Preserving Technologies in Data; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Information and Cyber Security

paper_title: A null model to detect coordinated online behavior integrating evidence from multiple indicators
summary: Coordinated online accounts can amplify messages and manipulate attention, but detecting such behavior is challenging due to confounding factors like account activity and item popularity.
abstract: Coordinated online accounts can amplify messages and manipulate attention, but detecting such behavior is challenging due to confounding factors like account activity and item popularity. We propose a statistical null-model framework that assesses behavioral similarity between accounts by comparing observed coordination indicators against activity- and popularity-conditioned reference distributions. By combining evidence across multiple indicators and partners, our method can identify suspicious coordination links more accurately. Evaluations on nine labeled information-operation datasets involving over 152 thousand accounts show that aggregating p-values multiplicatively across indicators and partners yields improved detection performance. While results vary across information operations, this approach offers a generalizable and statistically principled tool for uncovering coordinated online behavior.
topics: Misinformation and Its Impacts; Spam and Phishing Detection; Complex Network Analysis Techniques

paper_title: Temporal signatures of coordination: detecting and anticipating influence operations on social media
summary: Online influence operations (IOs) pose a critical threat to the integrity of public discourse on social media, yet their early detection and accurate prediction of user engagement remain open challenges.
abstract: Online influence operations (IOs) pose a critical threat to the integrity of public discourse on social media, yet their early detection and accurate prediction of user engagement remain open challenges. This work presents a comprehensive computational framework for understanding influence operations, addressing two interconnected questions: How can IO drivers be distinguished from legitimate users? And can future interactions between IO drivers and organic users be predicted? We analyze temporal interaction networks from five real-world influence campaigns attributed to state-sponsored actors from China, Cuba, Iran, Russia, and the United Arab Emirates. To motivate the importance of detecting IOs and predicting engagement with their content, we first provide empirical evidence that, in four of the five campaigns we study, organic user adoption of IO-pushed content (e.g., hashtags and URLs) is statistically associated with prior exposure to IO actors’ activity. Building on this evidence, we introduce two complementary modules: (i) IOBoost, a lightweight supervised classifier that leverages temporal, activity-based, and network motif features to identify IO driver accounts, achieving an average F1-score of 97.5%, demonstrating strong cross-campaign generalization and early detection capabilities for identifying IO drivers; and (ii) IOLink, a graph neural network model that leverages user interaction networks to predict future interactions between IO drivers and organic users, achieving an average ROC-AUC score of 86%. Our results reveal that coordinated influence campaigns leave distinctive behavioral traces in user adoption patterns and temporal interaction dynamics, enabling accurate and generalizable detection while remaining computationally efficient for real-world deployment. To ensure full reproducibility, we make the source code publicly available: https://github.com/SimoneMungari/IO-detecting-and-anticipating .
topics: Misinformation and Its Impacts; Spam and Phishing Detection; Complex Network Analysis Techniques

paper_title: Separation of Nonergodic Uniform Convergence Rates for Regularized Learning in Games
summary: Convergence of Optimistic Learning in Games and the Role of Forgetfulness Online learning algorithms solve games by repeatedly updating players’ strategies. A natural hope is that the latest strategy improves at a predictable rate.
abstract: Convergence of Optimistic Learning in Games and the Role of Forgetfulness Online learning algorithms solve games by repeatedly updating players’ strategies. A natural hope is that the latest strategy improves at a predictable rate. This paper shows that this intuition can fail for optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader methods, including the widely used optimistic multiplicative weights algorithm. In two-player zero-sum games, the authors separate three notions of nonergodic performance: last-iterate, random-iterate, and best-iterate convergence. They prove that no instance-independent last-iterate rate exists for the broad algorithmic family and establish strong lower bounds for random iterates. Yet, a useful positive result remains; in 2 × 2 games, optimistic multiplicative weights achieve a uniform best-iterate rate. The analysis traces the slowdown to a lack of “forgetfulness”; accumulated past losses can keep the dynamics moving away from equilibrium long after they reach its neighborhood. The results suggest that practitioners should distinguish carefully between the latest strategy, a randomly selected strategy, and the best observed strategy when evaluating learning dynamics.
topics: Game Theory and Applications; Advanced Bandit Algorithms Research; Stochastic Gradient Optimization Techniques

paper_title: Proximal Regret and Proximal Correlated Equilibria: A New Tractable Solution Concept for Online Learning and Games
summary: Learning and computation of equilibria are central problems in game theory, theory of computation, and artificial intelligence. In this work, we introduce proximal regret, a new notion of regret based on proximal operators that lies strictly between external and swap regret.
abstract: Learning and computation of equilibria are central problems in game theory, theory of computation, and artificial intelligence. In this work, we introduce proximal regret, a new notion of regret based on proximal operators that lies strictly between external and swap regret. When every player employs a no-proximal-regret algorithm in a general convex game, the empirical distribution of play converges to proximal correlated equilibria (PCE), a refinement of coarse correlated equilibria. Our framework unifies several emerging notions in online learning and game theory—such as gradient equilibrium and semicoarse correlated equilibrium—and introduces new ones. Our main result shows that the classic Online Gradient Descent (GD) algorithm achieves an optimal O(√T) bound on proximal regret, revealing that GD, without modification, minimizes a stronger regret notion than external regret. This provides a new explanation for the empirically superior performance of gradient descent in online learning and games. We further extend our analysis to Mirror Descent in the Bregman setting and to Optimistic Gradient Descent, which yields faster convergence in smooth convex games.
topics: Advanced Bandit Algorithms Research; Game Theory and Applications; Stochastic Gradient Optimization Techniques

paper_title: Near-Optimal Last-Iterate Convergence for Zero-Sum Games with Bandit Feedback and Opponent Actions
summary: Last-iterate convergence of learning dynamics in games has attracted significant recent attention. In two-player zero-sum games with bandit feedback, where only the loss of the selected action pair is observed, Fiegel et al.
abstract: Last-iterate convergence of learning dynamics in games has attracted significant recent attention. In two-player zero-sum games with bandit feedback, where only the loss of the selected action pair is observed, Fiegel et al. (2025) show a separation between average-iterate and last-iterate convergence in duality gap: while the optimal t^(-1/2) rate after t rounds is achievable for the former via standard no-regret algorithms, the latter cannot converge faster than t^(-1/3) in expectation or t^(-1/4) with high probability. However, in many practical settings, such as preference learning, the players observe not only their loss but also the opponent's action. This raises a natural question: can such additional information enable faster last-iterate convergence? We answer this question affirmatively, showing that t^(-1/2) last-iterate convergence is achievable with high probability in this setting, via an efficient algorithm that updates its strategy infrequently by solving an estimated log-barrier-regularized game. We identify fundamental obstacles preventing standard analysis for multi-armed bandits, the single-player case, from generalizing to games, and develop a novel analysis to overcome them. Experiments confirm that our algorithm indeed converges faster than naive baselines and prior methods that do not exploit opponent-action feedback. Finally, we note that our results also improve those for dueling bandits, a special case with skew-symmetric game matrices.
topics: Advanced Bandit Algorithms Research; Game Theory and Applications; Reinforcement Learning in Robotics

paper_title: The Challenges of Human-Centered AI and Robotics: What We Want, Need, and are Getting From Human-Machine Interaction
summary: Language-based AI is now ubiquitous, and user expectations for intelligent machines are scaling along with it: we expect machines to understand us, predict our needs and wants, do what we enjoy and prefer, and adapt as we change our moods and minds, learn, grow, and age.
abstract: Language-based AI is now ubiquitous, and user expectations for intelligent machines are scaling along with it: we expect machines to understand us, predict our needs and wants, do what we enjoy and prefer, and adapt as we change our moods and minds, learn, grow, and age. Physical AI, in the form of robotics, is the next major AI challenge, and it is not ready to leap into our daily lives yet. While massive investment is focused on functional behavior of humanoid robots (perceiving the world, moving around, and manipulating objects), human-robot interaction (HRI) is largely an afterthought, left for “later". This talk will discuss how bringing together robotics, AI, and machine learning for long-term user modeling, real-time multimodal behavioral signal processing, and affective computing is enabling machines to understand, interact, and adapt to users’ specific and ever-changing needs. We will overview methods and challenges of sparse and noisy heterogeneous, multi-modal, personal interaction data and of creating expressive agent and robot behavior toward understanding, coaching, motivating, and supporting a wide variety of user populations across the age span (infants, children, adults, elderly), ability span (typically developing, autism, anxiety, stroke, dementia), contexts (schools, therapy centers, homes), and deployment durations (from weeks to 6 months) through socially assistive robotics. We will discuss the challenges of understanding what we humans want from interactions with machines vs. what we need vs. what we are getting, and how those distinctions are shaping the future of not just AI and ML but society at large.
topics: Social Robot Interaction and HRI; Speech and dialogue systems; Emotion and Mood Recognition

paper_title: Multimodal Behavioral Typicality as a Training-Free Screening Signal for Dementia
summary: Dementia is commonly described as impairing what people attend to, say, and mean more than how they move their eyes or produce speech.
abstract: Dementia is commonly described as impairing what people attend to, say, and mean more than how they move their eyes or produce speech. We test this asymmetry with a cross-modal behavioral marker—negative log-likelihood (NLL) under frozen pretrained models across gaze, text, and audio—that separates semantic engagement from production mechanics without training on dementia data at any stage. On a new multimodal dataset of 39 participants (25 control, 14 dementia) performing the Cookie Theft task, semantic models separate control from dementia in gaze (Hedges’ g = 1.04) and text (g up to 1.31), with a smaller effect in linguistic speech (g = 0.66) that does not survive correction. Their mechanically-matched counterparts—bottom-up saliency and temporal gaze dynamics for gaze, an acoustic codec for audio—do not reach significance. For text, removing surface disfluencies strengthens rather than weakens the signal, indicating the effect does not reduce to fluency. The signal is model-independent: ten of eleven language models separate groups (g = 0.95 to 1.24). Three-way fusion reaches AUC = 0.94, and external validation on 549 DementiaBank Pitt Corpus transcripts replicates the direction across all eight autoregressive models tested. This is a screening signal rather than a diagnostic, and the implication for multimodal interaction systems is direct: adapt to semantic engagement, not production mechanics.
topics: Dementia and Cognitive Impairment Research; Neurobiology of Language and Bilingualism; Multimodal Machine Learning Applications

paper_title: LazySloth: Bounded LLM-based Lazy Tree Search for Fast Long Video Comprehension
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promising results in long-video understanding due to the rich semantic information they can capture.
abstract: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promising results in long-video understanding due to the rich semantic information they can capture. However, most methods focus on coarse captioning of extracted image frames that are computationally inefficient and require models with large context windows. While past work has explored efficient methods through multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), they rely on lossy embeddings that lose temporal context and fine-grained detail. Few works to date have investigated how VLM-based query-relevant information retrieval can be optimized. We introduce LazySloth, an efficient tree-based search method that speeds up video comprehension and retrieval tasks 2.9-8.3x (compared to existing agentic methods) through bounded captioning of portions of the video considered irrelevant by a VLM of the video. Compared to contemporary specialized video-understanding VLMs and RAG-based methods, LazySloth achieved similar or better final task accuracy across two recent open-source base VLMs--Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.6 27B--across four benchmarks. LazySloth reduced the gap between the base open-source model and a closed-source model, GPT-4o. Ablations showed that replacing VLM scene understanding with CLIP-based retrieval cost 8.8-19.9% in accuracy, while lazy tree construction matches eager construction at a fraction of the captioning cost. With LazySloth, we demonstrate the possibility of faster long-video comprehension without substantial loss in performance.
topics: Multimodal Machine Learning Applications; Video Analysis and Summarization; Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

paper_title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
topics: Natural Language Processing Techniques; Topic Modeling; Advanced Neural Network Applications

paper_title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
summary: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm.
abstract: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a systematic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navigation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20 settings. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, and fine-tuning approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience collected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses counterfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer. Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strategies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional retrieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models, showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.
topics: Reinforcement Learning in Robotics; AI-based Problem Solving and Planning; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior

paper_title: Toward Interactive Understanding of Code APIs
summary: Empowered by advances in Language Model agents, systems have made substantial strides in code generation and understanding. However, these approaches often rely on read access to the relevant code, an assumption which does not hold when dealing with external APIs.
abstract: Empowered by advances in Language Model agents, systems have made substantial strides in code generation and understanding. However, these approaches often rely on read access to the relevant code, an assumption which does not hold when dealing with external APIs. In this work, we introduce the PAU (Python API Understanding) benchmark, where we provide models with black-box, API-level access to code snippets. Models must query the API with exploratory inputs and draw insights from the resulting outputs, with the goal of describing the snippet's true functionality. By treating the code snippets as external tools that must be understood via interaction alone, PAU studies the more general problem of unsupervised tool understanding, specifically for tools implemented as Python methods. Despite recent progress in coding agents, even frontier models struggle to achieve high performance on PAU, with the best model (Claude-4-Opus) failing to understand over 45% of the PAU test set. An investigation into the common error modes reveals that models are overconfident; they often overrate the quality of their current hypothesis, leading to insufficient exploration and premature termination. Finally, we take inspiration from the Asymmetric Actor Critic (AAC) paradigm, frequently used in robot learning, to post-train models for interactive code understanding. Models trained with AAC conduct more active exploration of the APIs, with an AAC-tuned Qwen3-8B model matching the performance of GPT-5-mini.
topics: Software Engineering Research; Software Testing and Debugging Techniques; Topic Modeling

paper_title: Catalyst: Out-of-Distribution Detection via Elastic Scaling
summary: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical for the safe deployment of deep neural networks. State-of-the-art post-hoc methods typically derive OOD scores from the output logits or penultimate feature vector obtained via global average pooling (GAP).
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical for the safe deployment of deep neural networks. State-of-the-art post-hoc methods typically derive OOD scores from the output logits or penultimate feature vector obtained via global average pooling (GAP). We contend that this exclusive reliance on the logit or feature vector discards a rich, complementary signal: the raw channel-wise statistics of the pre-pooling feature map lost in GAP. In this paper, we introduce Catalyst, a post-hoc framework that exploits these under-explored signals. Catalyst computes an input-dependent scaling factor$(\gamma)$on-the-fly from these raw statistics (e.g., mean, standard deviation, and maximum activation). This$\gamma$is then fused with the existing baseline score, multiplicatively modulating it - an “elastic scaling” - to push the ID and OOD distributions further apart. We demonstrate Catalyst is a generalizable framework: it seamlessly integrates with logit-based methods (e.g., Energy, ReAct, SCALE) and also provides a significant boost to distance-based detectors like KNN. As a result, Catalyst achieves substantial and consistent performance gains, reducing the average False Positive Rate by 32.87% on CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18), 27.94% on CIFAR100 (ResNet-18), and 22.25% on ImageNet (ResNet-50). Our results highlight the untapped potential of pre-pooling statistics and demonstrate that Catalyst is complementary to existing OOD detection approaches. Our code is available here: https://github.com/bingabid/Catalyst.
topics: Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Anomaly Detection Techniques and Applications; Advanced Neural Network Applications

paper_title: DNN Modularization via Activation-Driven Training
summary: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) tend to accrue technical debt and suffer from significant retraining costs when adapting to evolving requirements. Modularizing DNNs offers the promise of improving their reusability.
abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) tend to accrue technical debt and suffer from significant retraining costs when adapting to evolving requirements. Modularizing DNNs offers the promise of improving their reusability. Previous work has proposed techniques to decompose DNN models into modules both during and after training. However, these strategies yield several shortcomings, including significant weight overlaps and accuracy losses across modules, restricted focus on convolutional layers only, and added complexity and training time by introducing auxiliary masks to control modularity. In this work, we propose MODA, an activation-driven modular training approach. MODA promotes inherent modularity within a DNN model by directly regulating the activation outputs of its layers based on three modular objectives: intra-class affinity, inter-class dispersion, and compactness. MODA is evaluated using three well-known DNN models and five datasets with varying sizes. This evaluation indicates that, compared to the existing state-of-the-art, using MODA yields several advantages: (1) MODA accomplishes modularization with 22% less training time; (2) the resultant modules generated by MODA comprise up to 24x fewer weights and 37x less weight overlap while (3) preserving the original model's accuracy without additional fine-tuning; in module replacement scenarios, (4) MODA improves the accuracy of a target class by 12% on average while ensuring minimal impact on the accuracy of other classes.
topics: Advanced Neural Network Applications; Software Engineering Research; Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning

paper_title: DAVIS: OOD Detection via Dominant Activations and Variance for Increased Separation
summary: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs is a critical safeguard for deploying machine learning models in the real world.
abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs is a critical safeguard for deploying machine learning models in the real world. However, most post-hoc detection methods operate on penultimate feature representations derived from global average pooling (GAP) -- a lossy operation that discards valuable distributional statistics from activation maps prior to global average pooling. We contend that these overlooked statistics, particularly channel-wise variance and dominant (maximum) activations, are highly discriminative for OOD detection. We introduce DAVIS, a simple and broadly applicable post-hoc technique that enriches feature vectors by incorporating these crucial statistics, directly addressing the information loss from GAP. Extensive evaluations show DAVIS sets a new benchmark across diverse architectures, including ResNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet. It achieves significant reductions in the false positive rate (FPR95), with improvements of 48.26\% on CIFAR-10 using ResNet-18, 38.13\% on CIFAR-100 using ResNet-34, and 26.83\% on ImageNet-1k benchmarks using MobileNet-v2. Our analysis reveals the underlying mechanism for this improvement, providing a principled basis for moving beyond the mean in OOD detection.
topics: Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Anomaly Detection Techniques and Applications

paper_title: Words that make SENSE: Sensorimotor Norms in Learned Lexical Token Representations
summary: While word embeddings derive meaning from co-occurrence patterns, human language understanding is grounded in sensory and motor experience.
abstract: While word embeddings derive meaning from co-occurrence patterns, human language understanding is grounded in sensory and motor experience. We present $\mathit{SENSE}$ ($\textbf{S}$ensorimotor $\textbf{E}$mbedding $\textbf{N}$orm $\textbf{S}$coring $\textbf{E}$ngine), a learned projection model that predicts Lancaster sensorimotor norms from word lexical embeddings. We also conducted a behavioral study where $281$ participants selected which among candidate nonce words evoked specific sensorimotor associations, finding statistically significant correlations between human selection rates and $\mathit{SENSE}$ ratings across $6$ of the $11$ modalities. Sublexical analysis of these nonce word selection rates revealed systematic phonesthemic patterns for the interoceptive norm, suggesting a path towards computationally proposing candidate phonesthemes from text data.
topics: Categorization, perception, and language; Embodied and Extended Cognition; Language, Metaphor, and Cognition

paper_title: Acoustic Cues Facilitate the Acquisition of Non-adjacent Dependencies in Sequences of Dynamic Object Transformation
summary: Human learners’ ability to detect rule-governed elements plays an important role in cognitive functions.
abstract: Human learners’ ability to detect rule-governed elements plays an important role in cognitive functions. While extensive research on the acquisition of regularities among adjacent items has provided robust and reliable evidence, learning structured patterns among non-adjacent components-known as non-adjacent dependencies (NADs)-remains far more tentative and only occurs under specific conditions. A past study by Lu and Mintz (2023) found that human learners need more training exposure to detect NADs in visual sequences of object transformations compared to sequences of human actions, but is unclear why. Building on this work, we present a series of three experiments to investigate whether learning NADs from visual dynamic sequences can be enhanced by maintaining the identifiability of the object throughout its transformations. In addition, we explore the effect of providing auditory information-speech or pure tones-along with the visual object transformation sequences. Our findings demonstrate that (a) NAD learning succeeded when speech cues co-occurred and matched with NAD-type frames but failed in the absence of auditory cues (Experiment 1); (b) pure tones presented contingently with the visual sequences also facilitated NAD learning (Experiment 2); and (c) regardless of whether speech or tones were used as additional cues, adult learners were unable to detect NADs when the relationship between specific auditory stimuli and specific visual object transformation sequences was disrupted (Experiment 3).
topics: Categorization, perception, and language; Visual and Cognitive Learning Processes; Multisensory perception and integration

paper_title: Measuring Ease of Reuse for Security Research Artifacts with Results-Reproduced Badges
summary: Reproducibility and reuse of scientific artifacts are critical for scientific progress. Artifacts that are easy to reuse help researchers compare results and build on prior work. Security conferences promote reproducibility through artifact evaluation and badging.
abstract: Reproducibility and reuse of scientific artifacts are critical for scientific progress. Artifacts that are easy to reuse help researchers compare results and build on prior work. Security conferences promote reproducibility through artifact evaluation and badging. The highest-level badge – results-reproduced – indicates that independent evaluators were able to use an artifact to reproduce key claims in the corresponding paper.
topics: Scientific Computing and Data Management; Security and Verification in Computing; Information and Cyber Security

paper_title: Data Flows in You: Benchmarking and Improving Static Data-flow Analysis on Binary Executables
summary: Data-flow analysis is a critical component of security research. Theoretically, accurate data-flow analysis in binary executables is an undecidable problem, due to complexities of binary code.
abstract: Data-flow analysis is a critical component of security research. Theoretically, accurate data-flow analysis in binary executables is an undecidable problem, due to complexities of binary code. Practically, many binary analysis engines offer some data-flow analysis capability, but we lack understanding of the accuracy of these analyses, and their limitations. We address this problem by introducing a labeled benchmark data set, including 215, 072 microbenchmark test cases, mapping to 277, 072 binary executables, created specifically to evaluate data-flow analysis implementations. Additionally, we augment our benchmark set with dynamically-discovered data flows from 6 real-world executables. Using our benchmark data set, we evaluate three state of the art data-flow analysis implementations, in angr, Ghidra and Miasm and discuss their very low accuracy and reasons behind it. We further propose three model extensions to static data-flow analysis that significantly improve accuracy, achieving almost perfect recall (0.99) and increasing precision from 0.13 to 0.32 for the GCC compiler, and achieving a recall of 0.86 with a precision increase from 0.12 to 0.22 for Clang. Finally, we show that leveraging these model extensions in a vulnerability-discovery context leads to a tangible improvement in vulnerable instruction identification.
topics: Security and Verification in Computing; Software Testing and Debugging Techniques; Advanced Malware Detection Techniques

paper_title: Position Paper: Living Artifacts: Enabling Vertical Progress in Cybersecurity Research
summary: Over the past decade, the cybersecurity research community has invested heavily in artifact evaluation to improve reproducibility. Conferences increasingly collect, evaluate, and award badges to research artifacts, such as code and datasets.
abstract: Over the past decade, the cybersecurity research community has invested heavily in artifact evaluation to improve reproducibility. Conferences increasingly collect, evaluate, and award badges to research artifacts, such as code and datasets. While these efforts have increased artifact availability and quality, they have not yet increased reuse nor led to vertical scientific progress, where research teams independently work on common problems and build upon each other's work. Artifact evaluation, as currently practiced, validates individual research claims, but does not create sustained, shared technical foundations for vertical scientific progress. In this position paper, we argue for a shift from artifact validation to artifact ecosystems and a practical path forward through what we call living artifacts. A living artifact readily deploys on public research infrastructure, and remains open to execution and versioned extension by the community. A living artifact is prepared by their authors on a public research infrastructure of their choice, and a copy of it is evaluated on the same infrastructure. Fixing the evaluation platform eases and standardizes artifact packaging and the evaluation process. Released artifacts are easily reused on the same infrastructure where they were evaluated. Living artifacts can be improved, extended, and ported over time, with explicit lineage linking original and derived versions. Artifacts that are actively reused evolve; others may become dormant, but remain accessible. We contend that living artifacts are a necessary next step for reproducibility in cybersecurity. By lowering barriers to reuse, enabling community-driven maintenance, and supporting longitudinal artifact evolution, they create the conditions for vertical progress in cybersecurity research.
topics: Scientific Computing and Data Management; Security and Verification in Computing; Information and Cyber Security

paper_title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies.
abstract: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.
topics: Multi-Agent Systems and Negotiation; Economic Theory and Institutions; Game Theory and Voting Systems

paper_title: The Conversation Turns First: Crowd Discussion and Price Reversals in Prediction Markets
summary: Prediction markets combine trading with public discussion of the same events. We examine whether comment-derived signals predict subsequent activity, buying direction, and changes in the leading outcome.
abstract: Prediction markets combine trading with public discussion of the same events. We examine whether comment-derived signals predict subsequent activity, buying direction, and changes in the leading outcome. A correlation sweep across 79 non-political Polymarket markets guides six classification experiments comparing comment features, trading features, and their combinations. On live blocks containing comments, attention nearly matches trading history in predicting heavy trading within 18 hours (PR-AUC 0.786 versus 0.790, against prevalence 0.606), with its relative advantage concentrated in short markets. Comment content carries directional information: toxicity ranks future buying direction above chance in 43 of 53 scored markets, while adding attention, sentiment, and stance to flow history increases ROC-AUC from 0.780 to 0.788. Leadership changes are predicted primarily by market state. Stance shifts against the leader before reversals in 23 of 27 evaluable markets, but adds no clear improvement in individual-block forecasting. These results distinguish attention from directional support and price uncertainty. They establish predictive associations consistent with discussion and trading responding to shared information, without identifying a causal effect of comments on markets.
topics: Sports Analytics and Performance; Stock Market Forecasting Methods; Financial Markets and Investment Strategies

paper_title: Causal Language in Post Titles Shapes Deeper Topological Structures of Online Conversations
summary: Causal reasoning is fundamental to human understanding and information organization. People prefer causal explanations because they offer coherence, predictability, and a sense of control.
abstract: Causal reasoning is fundamental to human understanding and information organization. People prefer causal explanations because they offer coherence, predictability, and a sense of control. Conversational structures shape how knowledge and perspectives are shared, validated, and amplified in networked publics. Understanding the structural effects of causal language can reveal pathways to fostering deeper, more meaningful interactions online. In this work, we investigate how causal language influences the topology and temporal evolution of discussion threads in online conversations with a dataset of 17 million posts across 200 subreddits in 2023 on Reddit. Our results show that causal language is consistently associated with deeper, more sustained conversations, with effects emerging early in the lifecycle of a thread, as demonstrated through a counterfactual experiment. Importantly, emotional responses do not differ substantially between causal language and non-causal language, suggesting that structural depth arises from framing itself rather than affective escalation. A lightweight qualitative analysis shows that causal framing titles prompt users to elaborate more with reasoning and contribute personal experiences, supporting deeper multi-turn exchanges. These findings suggest that causal language acts not merely as a stylistic device, but as a cognitively grounded and structurally influential signal that shapes the topological structures of online conversations.
topics: Expert finding and Q&A systems; Digital Communication and Language; Complex Network Analysis Techniques

paper_title: Reactive Decaborane Initiates Low-Temperature Polymer Decomposition and Drives Ceramic Formation
summary: Abstract Boron carbide (B4C) is a ceramic of considerable interest due to its high hardness, elevated melting point, excellent thermal stability, low density, and chemical inertness.
abstract: Abstract Boron carbide (B4C) is a ceramic of considerable interest due to its high hardness, elevated melting point, excellent thermal stability, low density, and chemical inertness. Decaborane-functionalized preceramic polymers (PCPs) prepared from ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) are excellent single-source precursors of B4C, but the mechanistic details for the decomposition and ceramic conversion during pyrolysis have been overlooked, preventing advances in redesigning preceramic polymers that have high char yields and desirable chemical compositions. Herein, we reveal insights into the role of decaborane during the polymer-to-ceramic transition of poly(cyclooctenyldecaborane) (PCD) to boron carbide. ROMP of the cyclooctenyldecaborane monomer enabled controllable molecular weight and produced a series of polymers with molecular weights up to 35 kg/mol and dispersities (D̵) in the range of 1.3-1.6. Thermogravimetric analysis coupled with infrared spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (TGA-IR and TGA-MS, respectively) of PCD revealed the evolution of small hydrocarbon species following an initial release of hydrogen at low decomposition temperatures around 250 °C, which is in stark contrast to the decomposition profile of unfunctionalized poly(cyclooctadiene) (PCOD) that transitions into volatile hydrocarbon species at approximately 450 °C. ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations support the experimental findings that hydrogen release from decaborane initiates the polymer-to-ceramic conversion. MD simulations indicate that the release of H2 results in the exothermic formation of boron clusters, which promote the thermal decomposition of the hydrocarbon polymer backbone. These findings indicate that decaborane plays an active role in the polymer-to-ceramic conversion rather than serving solely as a boron source, providing mechanistic insight that will enable the rational design of next-generation PCPs with enhanced ceramic yields and tunable compositions.
topics: Advanced ceramic materials synthesis; Boron Compounds in Chemistry; Boron and Carbon Nanomaterials Research

paper_title: Hydrogen Bonding in Supercritical Water Using Quantum Molecular Dynamics
summary: In supercritical water (SCW), defined as water above its critical point (Tc = 647K, Pc = 221 bar), the nature of hydrogen bonds remains a topic of great interest.
abstract: In supercritical water (SCW), defined as water above its critical point (Tc = 647K, Pc = 221 bar), the nature of hydrogen bonds remains a topic of great interest. While neutron scattering studies suggest a significant reduction in hydrogen bonding in SCW, quantum molecular dynamics (QMD) simulations indicate that hydrogen bonds persist but with altered properties. We use QMD simulations with density functional theory to investigate hydrogen bonding in SCW. We introduce an electron charge density overlap based criterion to define a cutoff for H-bonds, which proves robust under extreme conditions. QMD simulations at 1,000 K across a range of densities (0.1-1.0 g/cm3) reveal that a reduced level of residual hydrogen bonding persists in SCW. Our findings provide a useful and detailed understanding of the nature of the hydrogen bond and its dynamics, including H-bond lifetimes in supercritical water, offering insights for applications in chemistry, energy, and planetary sciences.
topics: Subcritical and Supercritical Water Processes; Spectroscopy and Quantum Chemical Studies; Phase Equilibria and Thermodynamics

paper_title: Multiparadigm Benchmark of Molecular Docking: From Physics to Co-Folding and Hybrid Models
summary: Generalizability of molecular docking predictions across novel protein targets and distinct small-molecule chemotypes is key to the successful application of deep learning co-folding approaches in drug discovery, as highlighted by recent benchmarks, including Runs-n-Poses [Škrinjar, P.; et al.Nat.
abstract: Generalizability of molecular docking predictions across novel protein targets and distinct small-molecule chemotypes is key to the successful application of deep learning co-folding approaches in drug discovery, as highlighted by recent benchmarks, including Runs-n-Poses [Škrinjar, P.; et al.Nat. Struct. Mol. Biol.2026, 33, 782-794.]. To compare generalizability across physics-based, hybrid rescoring models, and co-folding approaches, we systematically benchmarked several molecular docking tools representing these paradigms. Our results support previous observations that co-folding approaches show superior performance on targets resembling their training datasets. However, they deteriorate sharply to unacceptably low 20-40% success rates on novel dissimilar systems, consistent with memorization. In contrast, physics-based and hybrid methods exhibit greater out-of-distribution robustness, maintaining more than 60% success rates for docking protein-ligand complexes with minimal similarity to previously known complexes. Our results highlight the complementarity of AI-based approaches and methods based on physical sampling in all-atom models, in terms of their applicability range, and argue for the benefits of tighter integration.
topics: Computational Drug Discovery Methods; Protein Structure and Dynamics; Protein Degradation and Inhibitors

paper_title: PRECOG: Comprehensive Experimental Design and Stimuli Protocol for Investigating Depression and Suicidal Ideation
summary: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and n...
abstract: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and neurophysiological recordings. A total of 160 college-aged participants, including healthy controls, individuals with depression without suicidal ideation, and individuals with depression and suicidal ideation, were recruited based on screening using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Suicide Ideation Scale (SIS).The experimental protocol included three primary cognitive tasks: (1) an emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases toward affectively charged and suicide-related words, (2) a sentence processing task examining neural responses to self-referential statements varying in emotional and suicidal content, and (3) the Death-Brief Implicit Association Task (D-BIAT) to measure implicit associations with life and death. EEG and other physiological signals were recorded continuously throughout all tasks. Additionally, resting-state recordings (with eyes open and eyes closed) were obtained before, between, and after the emotional Stroop and sentence tasks.Neurophysiological data were acquired using 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electrocardiography (ECG), and galvanic skin response (GSR), and were supplemented with eye tracking and high-frame-rate facial video recordings. By integrating neural, behavioral, and physiological measures, the PRECOG study aimed to advance our understanding of cognitive and emotional processing in depression and suicidality, ultimately contributing to more precise risk assessment and targeted clinical intervention.
topics: Suicide and Self-Harm Studies; Neural and Behavioral Psychology Studies; Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

paper_title: PEDBench: Can Speech Models Detect Phonetic Errors?
summary: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention.
abstract: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention. Despite recent advances in speech models for phoneme recognition, their ability to reliably detect fine-grained phonetic errors remains unclear because of a lack of high-quality evaluation data. To address this gap, we introduce PEDBench, the first PED benchmark spanning a continuum from natural to controlled speech. It comprises real-world recordings of spoken errors made by children (N=334), scripted error productions by human actors (N=1,188), and synthetic error productions generated using phone-conditioned text-to-speech (N=1,083). All phonetic annotations were transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. Our evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art speech models shows that they fail to reliably detect phonetic errors, even under controlled conditions with acted and synthetic speech, where acoustic variability is reduced. The models also exhibit low precision, frequently misclassifying correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Our speech-language models, fine-tuned on synthetic data, outperform commercial and open-source baselines on word-level PED, although a sim-to-real domain gap remains. We plan to publicly release our code and recipes, along with our acted and synthetic datasets, to support the development of more accurate PED systems.
topics: Speech Recognition and Synthesis; Phonetics and Phonology Research; Speech and Audio Processing

paper_title: Towards Interpretable Framework for Neural Audio Codecs via Sparse Autoencoders: A Case Study on Accent Information
summary: Neural Audio Codecs (NACs) are widely adopted in modern speech systems, yet how they encode linguistic and paralinguistic information remains unclear.Improving the interpretability of NAC representations is critical for understanding and deploying them in sensitive applications.Hence, we employ Spar...
abstract: Neural Audio Codecs (NACs) are widely adopted in modern speech systems, yet how they encode linguistic and paralinguistic information remains unclear.Improving the interpretability of NAC representations is critical for understanding and deploying them in sensitive applications.Hence, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose dense NAC representations into sparse, interpretable activations.In this work, we focus on a challenging paralinguistic attribute-accent-and propose a framework to quantify NAC task-level interpretability.We evaluate 4 four NAC models under 16 SAE configurations using a relative performance index.Our results show that DAC and SpeechTokenizer achieve the highest interpretability.We further reveal that acoustic-oriented NACs encode accent information primarily in activation magnitudes of sparse representations, whereas phonetic-oriented NACs rely more on activation positions, and that low-bitrate EnCodec variants show higher interpretability.
topics: Speech Recognition and Synthesis; Speech and Audio Processing; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)

paper_title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision
summary: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world.
